narratives.ImplementationPlan: One product PR. In packages/core/src/install-health/owned-paths.ts, npmLockAppMetadataEqual ignores the top-level `name` (and any difference in it) when neither lockfile's root `packages[""]` entry carries a `name`: npm then derives that label from the folder, so it is package-manager metadata like `lockfileVersion` and `requires`. When the root entry carries a `name`, package.json declares one and a name change stays `mixed`. No change to the upgrade flow or to any installer file. Tests: owned-paths.test.ts (folder-derived name change is directive-only; app-declared name change is mixed; version change still mixed) and directive-only-drop.test.ts (a worktree-upgrade lockfile is dropped). Fragment: changelog.d/7233-lockfile-name-metadata.md. Generated and disclosure files in file_scope are predicted only; remove nothing if untouched.

narratives.Overview:
## Summary

The prospective scope-cover check (#5656 / #5771) refuses the commit for a plain `directive upgrade` when the upgrade runs in a folder whose name differs from the folder of the last lockfile write. The cause is the top-level `name` in `package-lock.json`.

When `package.json` has no `name`, npm writes the folder name into the lockfile's top-level `name`. `directive upgrade` runs npm, so an upgrade in a linked worktree (for example `.deft-scratch/worktrees/<folder>`) changes that field. `npmLockAppMetadataEqual` (`install-health/owned-paths.js`, via `classifyLockfile`) counts the top-level `name` as app metadata, so `classifyDirectiveOwnedChange("package-lock.json", …)` returns `mixed`. `package.json`, `AGENTS.md` and `.deft/GENERATION.json` in the same commit classify as `directive-only`, so the refusal names only the lockfile.

The suggested remedy (commit the Directive-only files, keep the lockfile out) leaves a commit whose pin does not match its lockfile. The operator had to commit the upgrade by hand.

Source: internal benchmark evidence (private). Directive 0.131.3 and 0.131.4 upgrades, Claude Code, Windows 11, npm 11, each upgrade in its own linked worktree from the default branch. Refused in both releases.

## Evidence

The upgrade's only lockfile changes were the runtime pin entries and the top-level `name` (`"<folder-A>"` → `"<folder-B>"`, both worktree folder names). Running the 0.131.4 ownership API on the committed blobs:

| Upgrade | Lockfile as committed | Same, top-level `name` restored |
|---|---|---|
| 0.131.2 → 0.131.3 | `mixed` | `directive-only` |
| 0.131.3 → 0.131.4 | `mixed` | `directive-only` |

So the top-level `name` is the only reason for the refusal.

## Expected

An upgrade that changes only Directive's dependency entries is `directive-only`, wherever it runs. Possible fixes (maintainer's choice):

- When `package.json` has no `name`, treat a change to the lockfile's top-level `name` (and an absent root `packages[""].name`) as package-manager metadata, like `lockfileVersion` and `requires`.
- Or have `directive upgrade` keep the lockfile's existing top-level `name`.

## Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] Given a project whose `package.json` has no `name`, when `directive upgrade` runs in a linked worktree with a different folder name, then the agent's commit of the upgrade deposit (pin, lockfile, generation record, managed AGENTS.md) passes scope-cover with no brief.
- [ ] Given a lockfile change that also changes the app's own `name` declared in `package.json`, then the verdict stays `mixed`.

## Related

#5771 (deposit-only commits), #6615 (ownership API), #6790 (the opposite precision gap: too permissive), #5949.
